site.title: Belgium Budget Builder
home.title: Where does Belgium's money go?
home.lede: Most of us have little sense of how big each part of public spending is. This site shows the 2026 budgets of all Belgian governments together, to scale: the federal government, social security, the regions and communities (Flanders, Wallonia, the Wallonia-Brussels Federation and Brussels) and, for completeness, local government. You can see how the topics relate, how hard it is to land a budget, and what choices mean over the next ten years. Money one government passes to another counts only once. The German-speaking Community is not included yet.
home.status: Under construction. Every figure will be sourced and reviewed before it is published.
map.title: Budget map
map.intro: Every rectangle is drawn to scale: twice the area means twice the money. Choose a government to see what it spends on.
map.transfersNote: Money one government passes on to another is shown only where it is finally spent, so nothing is counted twice.
map.nationalAccounts: In the national accounts (ESA, initial budget)
map.nationalAccountsWhy: The map shows the adjusted budget line by line, in payment credits, so the totals differ a little.
outlook.title: Ten-year outlook
outlook.intro: What happens to the public debt if the budget stays as it is, or as you set it above. Rising pension and healthcare costs from an ageing population are included.
outlook.balanceChange: Your change to the yearly balance
outlook.chartLabel: Public debt as a share of GDP, {from} to {to}
outlook.interestRate: Average interest rate on the debt
outlook.caveat: This is simple arithmetic, not a forecast. It does not model how people and companies react to tax or spending changes, nor interest rates that change over time. Ageing costs follow the official Study Committee on Ageing report; changing pension or healthcare spending scales their projected increase in the same proportion.
builder.fixed: Follows from the debt and interest rates (see the outlook)
ageing.title: The cost of ageing
ageing.intro: Compared with 2026, pensions and healthcare take a growing share of the economy, even if nothing else changes. These are the official projections of the Study Committee on Ageing; the extra cost is already included in the outlook above.
ageing.scaled: Your changes to pensions and healthcare in the map above also change this cost, in the same proportion.
ageing.chartLabel: Extra cost of ageing per year compared with 2026, in % of GDP, by pensions, healthcare and other, {from} to {to}
consequence.whereNote: Spread in proportion to the size of each part. A real reform chooses where to cut.
consequence.offset: matched by equal receipts, so cutting it alone saves nothing
consequence.howIntro: Spending like this changes through these levers. Each one is felt by someone different.

intro.label: Introduction
intro.s1.kicker: You read it in the paper
intro.s1.title: ‘Government looks for {amount} billion’
intro.s1.body: {amount} billion euros. It sounds like an enormous amount. But how much is it, compared with everything government spends?
intro.s2.title: This is everything
intro.s2.body: Together, Belgium's governments spend {total} in {year}: the federal government, social security, the regions, the communities and local government. Each dot is one billion euros.
intro.s3.title: These are the {amount} billion
intro.s3.body: That is {share} of all spending. Or about {perInhabitant} for every inhabitant, every year, babies and pensioners included.
intro.s4.title: But the gap is bigger
intro.s4.body: In {year}, governments together spend {deficit} more than they take in. That money is borrowed. {amount} billion closes {shareOfDeficit} of that gap; {rest} of deficit remains.
intro.s5.title: And the bill keeps growing
intro.s5.body: Interest on the debt already costs {interest} a year. It cannot simply be cut: it follows from the debt and interest rates. Without changes, debt rises to {debt} of GDP by {horizonYear}.
intro.s6.title: There are no easy choices
intro.s6.body: Behind every dot are pensions, hospitals, schools, police, trains and roads. Cuts affect people, so do taxes, and doing nothing lets the debt grow. Try to balance a budget yourself.
intro.why.title: How did we get here?
intro.why.body: According to the National Bank of Belgium, the deficit grew by {widening} between {from} and {to}. Leaving out interest, which fell, it grew by {primary}: {lowerRevenue} less revenue and {higherSpending} more spending, at the federal level ({federal}) and in the communities and regions ({regions}) alike.
intro.why.source: Source: National Bank of Belgium, Economic Review
consequence.effectsNote: Possible effects, not a forecast: who feels them depends on how the government makes the choice.
map.revenueIntro: What all Belgian governments together take in during 2026, by type, to scale. Lower or raise a type to see what it does to the deficit and the debt.
map.revenueNote: All governments together, consolidated, as the Federal Planning Bureau estimates them in the national accounts (ESA 2010). What one government passes on to another counts only once.
builder.revenueFixed: A bookkeeping entry: does not change the deficit
consequence.revenueEffectsNote: Possible ways, not a forecast: who pays more or less depends on how the government makes the choice. This site does not model how people and firms react.
consequence.levelsNote: Who collects it, before money passes between governments: the federal government, for example, passes part of what it collects on to the communities and regions and to social security. Source: Federal Planning Bureau, accounts per level of government.
footer.purpose: This site is not built for politicians: they should know these figures by heart. It is an effort to grow our shared understanding of public finances, makes no claim to be 100% correct, and is not a budgeting tool for governments.
